series.title: Reading Rickshaw Boy
series.deck: Three essays on defeated hopes, constrained choices, and a person who learns the calculation that has been used on him.
series.note: Based on the Chinese essays on Lao She’s Rickshaw Boy. Full-book spoilers.

articles.title: He Wanted a Rickshaw
articles.deck: A rickshaw, the savings for another, and a funeral: three defeats of an ordinary hope.
body: Xiangzi wanted a rickshaw.
At first, that was all. It was the whole of his plan.

Not to get rich, not to marry, not to buy land back in the country, not to become somebody. He wanted a rickshaw of his own, so that pulling it would no longer mean handing part of his earnings to its owner.

Lao She makes this wish very concrete. With his own rickshaw, he would pay no daily rental; he would not have to live at a yard owner's mercy; he could pull when he wanted to and rest when he did not.
He had worked out the figures. A new rickshaw cost around a hundred dollars. He saved day by day, for three years.
## How small the wish was
Pause here and consider the size of this wish.
A rickshaw cost roughly a hundred dollars at the time.
It was a sum a puller could save in three years by working and denying himself. It was not a dream. It was a commodity.
And what could this commodity bring him?
One less payment to make.
Most pullers rented their rickshaws. Each day they first paid the yard its share; only the remainder was theirs. Owning one meant no longer making that payment.
That was all.
He would still have to pull. Still run beneath the blazing sun and into the winter wind. Still bargain with fares and be looked down on. Nothing else about his life would change.
He wanted to keep the product of his labor, rather than hand over half of it every day.
It was about the smallest demand a person could make.
## And he was the best placed to do it
The beginning of the novel makes another point clear: among the pullers, Xiangzi was best equipped for the task.
He was young, in his twenties.
He was extraordinarily strong. Lao She spends a long passage on his body: tall, broad-shouldered, long-legged, able to run, with strength to spare. He describes him as being like a tree.
He did not drink, smoke, gamble, or visit brothels. These were four common drains on a puller's money, and he avoided all four.
He could endure hardship and was willing to do so. He pulled faster and longer than other men and never shirked.
He was honest, too. He did not snatch fares or take other men's work, or play tricks on people.
He possessed all the virtues available to a laborer at the bottom of that society.
What the novel would do next was render them ineffective, one by one.
## The first time
After three years, he had saved enough.
He bought his rickshaw.

The account of that day is among the brightest passages in the book. He remembered the date and decided to make it his birthday. He ran his hands over the rickshaw. It was his, bought with the sweat of his body.
Pulling it along the streets, he felt even the ground beneath his feet had changed.
Six months later, it was gone.
There was fighting outside the city. Someone offered a high fare for a journey to Tsinghua. The other pullers were afraid to go. Xiangzi thought of the money and went.
On the way, soldiers seized both him and the rickshaw.
They took the rickshaw away.
He was marched along and made to work for the troops for days. Eventually he escaped in the confusion, taking three camels with him. They gave him the nickname he would carry afterward.
He sold the three camels for thirty-five dollars.
Three years of savings had come back to him as thirty-five dollars.
## The second time
He began saving again.

This time he drove himself harder. Working as Mr. Cao's regular puller gave him a relatively settled life, and the money accumulated little by little. He kept his savings in an earthenware money jar, unwilling to entrust them to someone else.
This time, the man who took them was a policeman.

Detective Sun arrived saying that Mr. Cao was a political subversive and that arrests were to be made. Xiangzi would not escape either, he said, but for old acquaintance’s sake he would give him a way out.
He demanded all Xiangzi's money.
Xiangzi said it was the money for his rickshaw.
Sun said: if you do not hand it over, you come with me.
Xiangzi handed over the money from the jar.
In that scene, he cannot resist. The immediate threat turns his rickshaw savings into the price of getting away.
It is the money he has been putting aside to buy another rickshaw.
## The third time
The third time, hope again took the shape of a rickshaw, but someone else supplied the money.
Huniu bought it for him.

Huniu was the daughter of the yard owner, Fourth Master Liu, and more than ten years older than Xiangzi. She maneuvered him into a relationship and then pressured him into marriage. He married her against his wishes.
After their marriage, she used her private savings to buy a secondhand rickshaw from Er Qiangzi.
Xiangzi longed to have a rickshaw again, but he disliked this particular one.
Its history was bound up with a daughter sold and a wife dead; its black-and-white colors also struck him as unlucky. Yet the money was not his, and he felt unable to decide.
Later Huniu died in obstructed childbirth.
To pay for her funeral, he sold the rickshaw.
That was the third collapse of hope. The first two losses had been his own rickshaw and the savings to buy another.
## The shape of those three losses
Set the three events beside one another and look at what they share.
The first: soldiers.
The second: the police.
The third: a funeral.
What they share is this: their outcomes cannot simply be charged to his lack of diligence or thrift.

He was willing to work and to save. He did take a risk for the high fare to Tsinghua when other men refused. But that does not make the soldiers' seizure his wrongdoing, nor does avoiding such a risk guarantee a secure life.
He treated diligence and thrift as ways to hold on to a life.
The cruelest thing in the novel is that doing those things right did not protect what they produced.
He avoided drink and gambling, so he saved money. The money was taken.
He was strong and could endure hardship, so he pulled more than other men. The extra was taken.
He was honest and did not play tricks. That very honesty let Detective Sun approach him directly.
Within that arrangement, each virtue merely increased what could be taken from him.
## What was that arrangement?
We must now be clear about what was taking these things away.
It was not one particular villain.

The soldiers were not singling Xiangzi out: they seized rickshaws they encountered on the road. Sun's extortion was not personal either; it was how he lived. Today Xiangzi, tomorrow someone else. Huniu's death in childbirth was a calamity.
Taken together, the three events form something very clear.
In that environment, anything a laborer at the bottom managed to accumulate lay exposed.
He had no protection he could rely on.

He distrusted putting his money elsewhere and had few dependable avenues. Police protection was hardly available when the extortionist was a policeman. He lacked the money and knowledge to sustain a lawsuit. Even meeting someone willing to help did not give him a reliable system of safeguards.
From the first day he saved it, his money was liable to be taken by someone with a little power.
He did not understand that.
He thought that once he had saved enough, the rickshaw would be his.
## Something that must also be said
But this essay cannot speak only of what was taken from him. There is also something Xiangzi himself did.
After losing his first rickshaw, he took three camels.
They were someone else's camels. He took them while escaping and sold them for thirty-five dollars.
It was not robbery, nor much of a crime in this reading: it was something a man fleeing for his life did in a time of disorder.
It matters because it was the first time Xiangzi took something that was not his.
He felt a little unease, and it soon passed.
It is the first thread Lao She lays down.
For the novel will finally ask what this man becomes, and that change does not begin on one neatly marked day.
## What he thought
Between the three losses, Xiangzi's thinking was also changing.
After the first, his answer was: start again.
He gritted his teeth and planned to save from the beginning. If he worked hard enough, surely one day it would be possible. His spirit was still intact.
After the second, his answer was: there is no justice in this world.
Other thoughts began to enter. Men who did not work properly seemed to do well; what was he exhausting himself for? Yet he still did not give up.
After selling the rickshaw for the funeral, his spirit sank another level.
The change was not completed at the moment of that loss. Xiaofuzi would still give him the thought of beginning a new life.
But repeated disappointment was pushing him toward an idea: even selling his strength could not secure a life of his own.
## That judgment
Early in the book, Lao She offers a judgment that bears on the whole novel.
Its sense is this: Xiangzi thinks of his own rickshaw, his own life, everything resting on his own ability; yet this world will not allow a person to live that way.
There is another, harsher judgment after his collapse.
He had been respectable, ambitious, full of dreams, self-interested, individual, robust, magnificent Xiangzi.
Now he was a human failure.
Notice the word “individual.”
Lao She means something by it. Xiangzi's defining aspiration is to accomplish something alone.
He places his deepest trust in his own strength and dislikes staking his life on other people's help. He believes that being good enough will let him earn a life by himself.
The novel says that this road leads nowhere.
## Next
There were two women in Xiangzi's life.

One was Huniu: more than ten years older, unattractive, fierce, the yard owner's daughter. She maneuvered him into a relationship and pressured him to marry. She gave him a rickshaw and took possession of his days.
The other was Xiaofuzi, Er Qiangzi's daughter. Her father sold her; after she returned, she supported her two younger brothers by selling sex.
Both lived within even narrower limits than Xiangzi.
The next essay is about them.
Their role in this novel is not simply to provide a love story.
They are two instances of the ways a person can be disposed of.
Lao She, Rickshaw Boy, first serialized in 1936. The Chinese essay identifies the People's Literature Publishing House edition as its source.

articles.title: Huniu and Xiaofuzi
articles.deck: Two constrained lives, the price imposed on another person, and care without a return.
body: Huniu prepared the liquor and pressed Xiangzi to drink.
They were at the Harmony rickshaw yard, and her father was away. She had laid out food and drink and waited for Xiangzi to return. She had also dressed up for the occasion.
Xiangzi drank.
Amid the drink and the attraction, they had sex that night. The following morning, Xiangzi was ashamed and uneasy.
Some time later, Huniu told him she was pregnant.
## What happened
We must first be clear about this episode, because it is often simplified.
Huniu set a trap.
She was more than ten years older than Xiangzi and unattractive. The novel gives her a tigerish head, a dark face, and coarse speech. She was thirty-seven or thirty-eight and still unmarried.
Her father, Fourth Master Liu, would not let her marry.

His reason was practical. He owned the Harmony yard, with more than sixty pullers and a substantial business. Huniu ran it exceptionally well. Fierce, good with figures, able to keep the men in line, she was even more capable than her father.
He could not do without her.
So he delayed, year after year, until his daughter was thirty-seven or thirty-eight.
Huniu understood this perfectly well.
## Her position
Look at her position. The novel treats her harshly, sometimes with justification and sometimes unfairly.
Lao She makes her ugly on the page.
He writes of her appearance, her coarseness, her calculations, her deception of Xiangzi, and then her laziness, eating, and ordering others about. Almost nowhere is she depicted sympathetically.
Yet her situation is this.
She is thirty-seven or thirty-eight, unmarried, managing a business for her father in his household.
Her ability sustains the yard, but control of it remains with him. She has private savings; they have not given her a business or a life she can arrange for herself.
Her father decides whether she marries, and he has no intention of letting her.
Marriage would cost the yard a worker who works for nothing.
In other words, her position belongs to the same category as Xiangzi's.
Other people take Xiangzi's strength. Her father takes Huniu's ability.
Xiangzi can at least save, dream, and plan to buy a rickshaw of his own.
Huniu hopes marriage will allow her a different life, and her father blocks that road.
## So she chose that method
Her method was to act first and force acceptance afterward.
She chose Xiangzi.
Why him? The novel gives her reasons. He was young, strong, honest, capable, free of drink and gambling. He also had no family or backing, which made him easy to control.
She brought her plan about.
She was pregnant—or so she claimed. The novel later reveals that the first pregnancy was a lie, with a pillow used to simulate it. Later, she really did become pregnant.
She tried to force her father's agreement. When he refused, she broke with him, took her private savings, and moved out with Xiangzi.
She had succeeded.
The marriage she had chosen in defiance of her father took place.
## And the cost
The cost was Xiangzi.

He did not want to marry her. At the drinking party, he was pressured and also experienced desire; that did not put a yard owner's daughter and a puller without backing on equal ground. The false pregnancy and pressure to marry then pushed him into a life he did not want.
Her situation cannot erase what she did.
She used on another person the very method she most hated.
Her father treated her as a supply of labor, so she wanted out. Her way out was to treat Xiangzi as a ticket she could use.
The qualities she selected—young, strong, honest, without backing—take the same form as a livestock buyer's specifications.
Both things are true. They do not cancel each other.
Her situation was narrow. And in forcing her way out, she stepped on another person.
## Her life afterward
The novel makes the married Huniu look particularly bad.
She stopped working.

She had spent half her life managing the yard. Once outside it, she did nothing: lay about, ate, ordered Xiangzi around, complained. She would not let him pull a rickshaw. Her husband must not do such lowly work, she said.
Xiangzi could not stand it.
But this passage deserves a closer look. Why did Huniu stop working?
Because at last she could.
She had managed her father's yard for years without controlling the business. Now she had her private savings, a man, and a room of her own.
This was what she wanted: a stretch of life without work and without having to live at someone else's mercy.
She had less than a year of it.
## How she died
She died in obstructed childbirth.
The novel places her age, her first pregnancy, and her eating much and moving little within its account of the difficult birth.
Help was also delayed, stage after stage.

The midwife who came first could not deliver the child. Then Second Granny Chen was called in to perform her spirit rituals; money was spent to no effect. Finally Xiaofuzi went to the hospital to ask about care. She returned with the cost of a consultation and the greater cost of admission. Xiangzi could not raise it.
The child did not survive either.
To pay for the funeral, Xiangzi sold the rickshaw.
This was the third loss of hope described in the first essay.
## Xiaofuzi
The other woman's circumstances were different.
Xiaofuzi was Er Qiangzi's daughter.
Er Qiangzi was a puller who drank and had a vicious temper.
He first sold Xiaofuzi to an army officer.
He received two hundred dollars. Later, drunk, he kicked and beat his wife. She was injured, took to her bed, and eventually died.
The following spring, the officer left and abandoned Xiaofuzi.
She came home.
At home, her father drank and neglected everything, and her two younger brothers were small and hungry.
So she began selling sex.

At first Huniu lent her room for the purpose and took twenty cents each time. Later, when she refused to lend it, Xiaofuzi had to return to her own miserable room. Her earnings had to put food into her brothers' mouths.
Her father knew and used her money to drink.
## What she did
There is something about Xiaofuzi that the novel writes very lightly.
She keeps caring for people.
She cares for her two brothers and bears the household burden her father leaves. The man who beat his wife to death and sold his daughter still takes what the daughter earns to buy drink.
She is good to Xiangzi.
After Huniu's death, they draw close. She tells him she is willing to make a life with him.
He does not accept.
His reason is practical: he cannot support them. There are her two brothers and her father. He has just sold his rickshaw and has nothing.
He tells her he will come back when he has found a way.
Then he leaves.
## When he comes back
Later, Mr. Cao gives Xiangzi a renewed prospect of making a life, and he wants to find Xiaofuzi and share it with her.
He goes looking.
She is no longer there.
He learns that she has been driven into the White House, a brothel at the very bottom of the trade.
She stayed there for a time.
Then she hanged herself in the woods.
After hearing of her death, Xiangzi goes to a burial ground among pine trees and sits down.
He knows it is not her grave. Still, he weeps.
## Two ways of disposing of a person
Put these women beside one another. They are two different instances.
Huniu is kept.
She is able and resourceful, and her father keeps her ability for twenty years. She is not sold but retained, not allowed to leave, because she is too useful.
Her way of breaking out is to turn another person into a tool.
Xiaofuzi is sold.
She can scarcely determine where she goes. Her father sells her; the officer discards her; later she is again forced into a life of selling sex.
The crucial positions in her life are repeatedly disposed of by others.
And she keeps caring for people.
What these women share is the difficulty of holding their own abilities and bodies in their own hands.
Huniu's ability belongs to the yard. Xiaofuzi's body belongs to her father's drinking money.
The difference is that Huniu sees through the arrangement and acts. Xiaofuzi sees through it but has nowhere from which to act.
## The weight of Xiaofuzi's action
We should stay with Xiaofuzi a little longer. Something in her story is easily missed.
She keeps caring, without a return.
She cares for her brothers. Will they remember her when they grow up? The novel does not say.
She supports her father, the man who sold her.
She is good to Xiangzi. Xiangzi leaves, with reasons for leaving.
Nothing she does buys her anything.
Yet she goes on doing it for years.
Until she walks into those woods.
In this reading, it is the one kind of action the book's machinery cannot explain.
Xiangzi pulls to buy a rickshaw. Huniu schemes to escape. Er Qiangzi sells his daughter for drinking money. Fourth Master Liu keeps his daughter for the yard.
Each can be calculated.
Xiaofuzi's care for the father who sold her cannot.
## Xiangzi's choice
There is one last, uncomfortable thing to say.
Xiangzi does not take Xiaofuzi as his partner because he cannot afford to support her family.
The reason is real.
She, her two brothers, and their father: a single puller could scarcely support that household. These are not empty words.
And here Lao She writes with extraordinary precision.
At that moment, Xiangzi is thinking about his rickshaw.
He has just sold the secondhand one Huniu bought. He still wants to save again. To him, marrying Xiaofuzi means that feeding the household will consume the hope of buying a rickshaw.
He is making a calculation.
In his own eyes it is legitimate, clear-headed, and necessary.
And it is.
The problem is that, in the novel's movement, this is the first time Xiangzi puts a person into an account and calculates.
The first essay discussed the three camels. That was the first thread.
This is the second.
## Next
After Xiaofuzi's death, Xiangzi collapses completely.
But the novel continues.
Lao She does not let him die. He gives him neither a great awakening nor any respectable conclusion.
He lets Xiangzi live, and writes what that person becomes.
That is the subject of the next essay.
For it is what the novel is really telling us, and it is not a story of someone becoming poor.
It is a story of someone becoming something else.

articles.title: He Is Still Alive
articles.deck: Not simply becoming poor: a man learns to turn another person into a sum of money.
body: After Xiaofuzi died, Xiangzi did not.
The book continues for a long while.
Lao She does not let him die in the snow, does not give him a great awakening, does not provide any ending worthy of the name.
He leaves the man alive, then writes, page after page, what he becomes.
And this is the novel's real subject.
## He began to drink
First, look at the concrete changes.
He drank.

As the first essay said, one of Xiangzi's greatest resources had been abstaining from drink, tobacco, gambling, and brothels. These were the four common ways a puller's money drained away. He avoided them all.
Now he did all four.
He smoked. He drank. He gambled. He went to brothels.
His body, too, had already been damaged.

While working for the Xia household, he had contracted a disease and spent money on treatment. Before news of Xiaofuzi's death arrived, his body and his life had already been wearing away, layer by layer.
## He began to shirk
He stopped pulling properly.
Once he had run faster and longer than anyone. Now he rested whenever possible and avoided any journey he could.
He began to play dirty.
The novel describes his later methods: he would agree on a fare, then demand more at the destination and refuse to leave unless it was paid. He learned the very practices he had once most despised.
He began taking advantage of others.
Snatching fares, stealing business, quarreling. Once he played no tricks; now he had more tricks than anyone.
## He began to deceive
He started borrowing money without repaying it.
He borrowed everywhere, from anyone, and then denied the debt. He became adept at it, knowing how to soften a heart and what to say to each person.
He also learned to look pitiable on purpose.
He knew what his condition could obtain and began exchanging it for money.
He worked as a procession attendant at weddings and funerals, carrying flags and other objects. The former Xiangzi would have looked down on the work. By the end, he could not even do this properly.
Dragging himself along, he grabbed the lighter objects to carry, fell out of formation, and was cursed and struck.
## The decisive act
At the end of the book comes an action that brings its movement to a point.
Xiangzi informed on someone.
The man was Ruan Ming, who had appeared earlier in connection with Mr. Cao: a student involved in political agitation who later held a minor official position. He had had some dealings with Xiangzi.
Xiangzi denounced him.
For sixty dollars.
The novel is clear. He knew that informing on the man would bring money. He went and got it.
The man was paraded through the streets and later shot.
What did Xiangzi do with the money?
He later went to the White House, trying to anesthetize the fear inside him.
He did not regret informing, but he was afraid. With the money hidden on him, he felt as though a ghost were following him.
## This is not becoming poor
Now we come to the point of this essay.
This whole movement is often read as life destroying a good man.
That reading is too gentle.
Xiangzi did not become poor.
He had always been poor. At the beginning, he was poor enough to need three years of saving for a rickshaw. Poverty is not the change.
Nor is the change simply laziness.
Laziness is a matter of degree. A person can be a little lazier or a little more diligent and remain the same person.
He becomes something else.
Look at the informing.
After his first rickshaw was taken, he thought of beginning again.
After the extortion, he thought that there was no justice in the world.
This time, he went and earned sixty dollars.
In his eyes, the man named Ruan Ming was sixty dollars.
That is what the change consists in.
He has learned to convert a person into a number.
## Where he learned it
And this method has a source.
Xiangzi has been converted into figures many times.
When the soldiers seized him and his rickshaw, he was a laboring body and a vehicle. They did not ask his name or what he intended to do. They saw something that could pull things.
When Detective Sun extorted him, he was cash that could be squeezed out. Sun assumed he had savings and knew that he was afraid to resist and had no backing.
When Huniu selected him, as the second essay described, she chose youth, strength, honesty, and the absence of backing. It was a list of specifications.
When Fourth Master Liu looked at him, he saw a puller who could earn money.
For years, other people had calculated what this person was worth to them.
At last he learned the calculation and used it on somebody else.
Sixty dollars.
## What Lao She wrote
Lao She leaves one of the novel's most famous judgments.

Its sense is this: respectable, ambitious, dreaming, self-interested, individual, robust, magnificent Xiangzi had accompanied countless other people's funerals. Who knew when or where he himself would be buried—this fallen, selfish, unfortunate offspring of a diseased society, this dead end of individualism?
The sequence of words deserves to be read one at a time.
“Dead end of individualism” is usually read as Lao She's criticism of individual striving.
But look closely at the first string of terms: respectable, ambitious, dreaming, robust. These praise him.
Among them sits another word: self-interested.
And in the latter part there is a corresponding word: selfish.
Throughout this man's life, Lao She sees two sides of the same thing.
Xiangzi's ambition and his self-interest belong together.
The first essay argued that his defining aspiration is to accomplish something alone.
He trusts his own strength most and dislikes staking his life on other people. He thinks that working hard enough will let him earn a life for himself.
That pride and his eventual solitary decay grow from the same root.
Someone who always wants to stand by himself finds it difficult, when he falls, to find a connection strong enough to catch him.
## The passage about Old Ma
Old Ma's story makes the lone individual's predicament particularly clear. It begins early, but the grasshopper image comes only at their later reunion.
He is an old puller, surnamed Ma.
Xiangzi first encounters him in a teahouse. The old man has pulled all his life and has a little grandson with him. He is nearly overcome by the cold.
Xiangzi buys him ten mutton buns.
When they meet again, the grandson has been dead for over six months. Old Ma has sold his rickshaw and now sells tea. It is then that he speaks.
His meaning is roughly this: if you want to know what a lifetime of pulling leaves you in old age, look at me.
He also gives an image: grasshoppers.
One grasshopper may leap high, but a child can put out a hand and catch it. When they form swarms, moving in great sheets, no one can stop them; they can eat a whole field of crops bare.
Those who sell their strength, he says, are like the solitary grasshopper.
Here someone puts before Xiangzi the possibility of something beyond going it alone.
Xiangzi understands. The novel says he truly understands: he is the grasshopper tied by a string.
Yet understanding the lone person's helplessness does not lead him onto another road.
He too sinks into hardship, then does something Old Ma has not done: he exchanges another person for money.
## Why the book ends this way
Now for this essay's final judgment.
The book offers no conclusion.
Its last sentence concerns that dead end. Xiangzi has not died, awakened, or turned his life around. There is no accounting that settles his story.
He remains in the city, alive, still going down.
This form is necessary, for two reasons.
First, if Xiangzi died, the book would become a tragedy, and tragedy has a shape.
A person strives, fails, and dies. That is a complete shape. Readers can grieve and close the book. Grief can bring an ending.
Lao She withholds it.
He lets the man live and decay a little more each day.
Second, and more importantly, if Xiangzi died, the question of what he became would no longer have to be answered.
Yet that is precisely what the novel wants to answer.
It is not writing only the process by which a person is destroyed.
It writes what remains after the destruction.
The answer is something still walking, still borrowing, still deceiving, still capable of denouncing someone for sixty dollars.
It looks exactly like Xiangzi.
## What has not been taken
But this essay cannot end there. Something else in the novel has not entered the calculation.
Those three years.
The three years in which Xiangzi saved his first sum were real. He ran day after day and saved coin after coin, avoided drink and gambling, and made his life into a taut string.
Every day of those years was his own.
No one forced or supervised him. While he saved the money, the act was in his hands.
The rickshaw was later taken. Those three years cannot be taken.
And there is something else.
He bought Old Ma ten buns.
He had little money, the old man had no connection to him, and the purchase would bring nothing in return.
He bought them.
The second essay spoke of Xiaofuzi supporting the father who had sold her. That act does not balance out.
Nor does Xiangzi buying buns for Old Ma.
In this book, whatever can be calculated is eventually gathered up by that machinery.
The few things that cannot be calculated have not been gathered up, because they never stood in any account.
## Finally
The three essays can now be placed together.
A man wants a rickshaw. It is about the smallest demand a person can make: to keep the product of his labor rather than surrender half of it each day.
He has the best qualifications for his trade: youth, strength, abstinence from drink and gambling, endurance, honesty.
Those virtues do not protect what they produce.

Three hopes, three defeats: soldiers seize his own rickshaw, the police extort his savings for another, and Huniu's secondhand rickshaw is sold for her funeral. These outcomes cannot be charged simply to insufficient diligence or thrift. Within that arrangement, his virtues only increase what can be taken.

There are two women beside him. One is prevented from marrying because she is too useful; she escapes by treating another person as a ticket. The other is sold by her father and later forced into selling sex, yet keeps caring for others, including the man who sold her.
Then he collapses.
The book does not let him die.
He drinks, gambles, borrows without repaying, and learns every practice he once despised. Finally, he denounces a man for sixty dollars.
That is not becoming poor, or merely becoming lazy.
It is learning to convert a person into a number. The method is taught by those who have spent his life calculating him.
On the novel's final page, the man is still alive.
He is still walking through that city.

Lao She, Rickshaw Boy, first serialized in Yuzhou Feng in 1936. The Chinese essay identifies the People's Literature Publishing House edition and the full ending preceding Lao She's later revisions as its source.
